claims.head: The Avalanche should tilt the ice
claims.body: At 5-on-5, the Avalanche have been one of the league’s best at getting more of the chances than they give up, and the Maple Leafs one of the worst. The ice should tilt the Avalanche’s way, even if goaltending and bounces have the final say on the score.

notes.text: Zachary L'Heureux is no longer killing penalties: 3% of the team’s shorthanded time in 3 games, down from 36% with his old team last season.
Kirill Marchenko is on injured reserve and has missed the last 3 games. He is one of their most valuable skaters.
Nick Blankenburg is out week to week (upper body injury) and has missed the last 5 games. He is one of their more valuable skaters. Troy Stecher has taken his spot beside Oliver Ekman-Larsson.
John Tavares is day to day (lower body injury) and has missed the last 9 games. He is one of their more valuable skaters.
Max Domi is on long-term injured reserve and has not played this season.
Dakota Mermis was added to the roster on Oct 24 and has played beside Oliver Ekman-Larsson.
Oliver Ekman-Larsson has started killing penalties: on the ice for 29% of the team’s shorthanded time in 17 games, up from 6% last season.

stakes: The Avalanche go in tied for third in the Central with 20 points, the Maple Leafs seventh in the Atlantic with 18 points.

TOR.head: Not an easy night for the Maple Leafs
TOR.body: Even though Toronto has home-ice advantage, Colorado has been out-chancing opponents by a wide margin lately. On top of that, Toronto will be without Marchenko. The Maple Leafs’ best way through is keeping dangerous shots away.

COL.head: Advantage, the Avalanche
COL.body: Even though Toronto has home-ice advantage, Colorado has been out-chancing opponents by a wide margin lately. On top of that, Toronto will be without Marchenko. The Maple Leafs’ way back in is keeping dangerous shots away.

story.head: MacKinnon’s favorite opponent
paras: The Maple Leafs won the teams’ first meeting this season, 6-3 in Colorado on Oct 10. The Avalanche (9-6-2) lost 3-2 in overtime to Nashville on Thursday, and the Maple Leafs (8-7-2) lost 3-2 to Utah on Nov 3. Going in, the Avalanche are fourth in the Central (tied for 11th in the NHL) and the Leafs seventh in the Atlantic (19th).
The Avalanche’s record (.588) is about what their chances are worth. The Maple Leafs’ record (.529) is running ahead of what their chances are worth (.478), largely thanks to their finishing.

The Avalanche ice the puck less than anyone (1st) and do a lot of their shooting from distance (lowest). Colorado has scored 4.00 goals a game, the second most in the league. As for the Maple Leafs, they get their shots through better than anyone (1st), but take more penalties than they draw (31st) and take a lot of low-quality shots (31st). The Avalanche are likely to get plenty of pucks to the net against the Maple Leafs. On top of that, both teams like to play fast, especially the Avalanche (1st), so expect an open game.

Nathan MacKinnon (9 G / 18 A / 27 P in 17 GP) leads the Avalanche in scoring and is fifth in the NHL, with a point in seven straight games against Toronto. Artturi Lehkonen (12 G / 5 A / 17 P in 17 GP) has a team-high twelve goals, tied for fourth in the NHL. Auston Matthews (11 G / 15 A / 26 P in 17 GP) leads the Maple Leafs in scoring and is tied for sixth in the NHL, with eight points in his last five games. William Nylander (10 G / 11 A / 21 P in 17 GP) isn’t far behind.

Mackenzie Blackwood (8-3-1 / .893 SV% in 12 GS) will likely start for Colorado. Toronto has two options in net: Sergei Bobrovsky (3-6-2 / .889 SV% in 11 GS) and Anthony Stolarz (5-1-0 / .910 SV% in 6 GS). Bobrovsky has started seven of their last ten games, including the last one on Nov 3, so Toronto could turn to Stolarz to give him a rest. It’s anyone’s guess who gets the net.
The Avalanche usually control more of the chances than the Maple Leafs do.
